text:
matt: quick q — running very short nsys captures (~400-600ms) and seeing kernel selection flip right after KV warmup. flags I'm using: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o out.qdrep --capture-duration 0.5`

sara: short captures are risky. warmup can move you into a different kernel path (prefetch vs fastpath). try bracketed captures to isolate warmup vs steady state.

matt: any recommended CLI incantation for bracketed?

sara: yeah, two captures is simplest: warmup window then steady window. e.g.

```
# warmup (0..3s)
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o warmup.qdrep --capture-range=timerange:0..3 ./workload
# steady-state (3..13s)
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o steady.qdrep --capture-range=timerange:3..13 ./workload
```

sara: that gives you clear before/after timelines to compare KV cache hits and kernel timelines.

devon: also: avoid tiny sample windows. if you rely on sampling the kernel switch can be missed or biased. for short experiments try: disable sampling (full trace) or increase capture duration. `--sample=none` (or use `--sample=cpu` depending on version) so you capture every kernel event.

devon: another trick — add an explicit synthetic warmup in the workload so the runtime actually reaches steady-state before you start the steady capture. eg run 2 warmup batches with `--dry-run` like behaviour.

matt: got it. is it useful to enable osrt + nvtx together? I'm currently using `trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt` because we emit NVTX ranges from runtime.

sara: yes, keep nvtx for range context. osrt helps with host-side scheduling traces and can show when batching gets delayed by other threads. cuda + nvtx + osrt is the usual combo for kernel timeline + batching + qt cache handoffs.

devon: watch out for file size when you do full traces — qdrep can be huge. compress or limit with more focused capture ranges. also set `--capture-fork-children=true` if your workload spawns processes.

matt: any heuristics for where kernel selection happens? I'm seeing a short-lived kernel that repeats ~10x then disappears when KV hits increase.

sara: that pattern screams cold-KV fallback: first requests miss, small kernel path used (prefetch/naive matmul), once KV fills, the more optimized kernel (prefetch-merged/kv-fast) takes over. look at per-kernel duration and occupancy in the timeline, and inspect NVTX ranges for "kvcache.fill" or similar.

devon: in the timeline filter by CUDA kernel name + duration > 1us and sort by start time. if you have the sqlite export you can do quick queries to count kernel invocations pre/post warmup.

```
# example: export to sqlite and run a quick SQL to compare counts
nsys export --report=sqlite -i steady.qdrep -o steady.sqlite
sqlite3 steady.sqlite "select name, count(*) from cuda_kernels group by name order by count desc limit 20;"
```

matt: neat. I'll try bracketed captures + full trace for warmup and a sampled (longer) steady capture. any recommended capture-duration numbers?

sara: depends on batch size and input length — for our microbenchmarks we do ~3s warmup + 10-30s steady. for prod-like latency traces aim for several hundred steady requests (so 10-60s).

devon: one more: if you suspect kernel switching due to sequence length, run two experiments with short and long sequences keeping batch size constant. that often changes kernel selection thresholds.

ci-bot: capture uploaded: https://artifacts.internal/redwood/traces/1705001234/out.qdrep :thumbsup:

matt: awesome — thanks, running bracketed + longer steady now. will post results. :rocket:
